title: Psalms (Part 1)
hook: There's a Hebrew word tucked into the first verse of the Psalter that never quite makes it into English: *ashre* is plural, literally "happinesses of," as if ordinary blessedness couldn't hold what the psalmist meant. That single word sets the tone for a collection that refuses to stay in the register of tidy devotion—these are songs written by a king who knew both throne rooms and caves, who could look at the heavens "pouring forth speech" in Psalm 19 and, just chapters later, ask God why He had forsaken him. Psalm 2 goes so far as to put words in God's own mouth to His anointed—"Thou art my Son"—language of covenant and enthronement that the New Testament writers couldn't stop quoting when they tried to describe Christ. What makes this stretch of Psalms remarkable isn't just its poetry; it's the honesty—flourishing and despair, creation's silent testimony and the soul's loudest complaints, all held together in the same sacred songbook. Spend time this week with the man who is like a tree planted by rivers of water, and you may find your own roots going down a little deeper.
